Banz Monastery, with its 900 years of history, is located in the valley of the River Main in Upper Franconia. In about 1069 or 1071, Countess Alberada and her husband, Margrave Hermann of Vohburg, donated their castle on Mount Banz to the Benedictines as a monastery.In the Thirty Year War, the abbey was destroyed; between 1698 and 1780, it was rebuilt and extended first by Leonhard Dientzenhofer, and then, after his death, by Johann Dientzenhofer and Balthasar Neumann, to become one of the biggest monasteries in Bavaria. When the abbey closed as a result of secularisation, the monastery’s last glorious era came to an end. In 1814, Duke Wilhelm of Bavaria acquired Banz as his summer residence. Before being taken over by the Hanns Seidel Foundation as a meeting and education center in 1978, the monastery was in the possession of the missionary order of the „Society of the Holy Angels“. After extensive renovation and restoration work, the completion of Banz Monastery was celebrated in 1990.There are now 180 beds available for participants attending events; for conference work, there are twelve seminar rooms for groups of 15 to 300 persons. 发布源: Heinrich Böll Stiftung -- Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-26

The Heinrich Böll Foundation maintains close ties to the German Green Party (Alliance 90/The Greens) and as a think tank for green visions and projects, we are part of an international network encompassing partner projects in approximately 60 countries.

Heinrich Böll's encouragement of civil society interference in politics is a model for the work of the foundation. Its primary task is political education in Germany and abroad to promote the democratic will, the socio-political commitment and international understanding. It is guided by the basic political values of ecology, democracy, solidarity, and nonviolence. The foundation is particularly interested in the realization of a democratic immigration society as well as gender democracy as a relationship of the sexes that is free of dependence and domination.

In addition, the foundation promotes art and culture as an element of its political educational work and as an expression of social self-understanding. Currently, the study program of the Heinrich Böll Foundation supports about 1.200 students and doctoral candidates with scholarships. The general meeting, consisting of 49 persons, is the supreme decision-making body and chooses a. o. the board.

Presently, the full-time executive board is formed by Dr. Imme Scholz and Jan Philipp Albrecht. The management is held by Steffen Heizmann. The statutes provide for a quotation for women and migrants for the Foundation's bodies and the full-time positions.

Unsere Abteilung analysiert verschiedene Kooperationsformen, darunter Nord-Süd-, Süd-Süd- und triangulare Partnerschaften, mit einem polit-ökonomischen Fokus von Kooperationsstrukturen und Entwicklungspolitik. Wir untersuchen sich wandelnde Konzepte wie den „Globalen Süden“ und erforschen innovative Beispiele wie etwa interurbane Zusammenarbeit in arktischen Regionen. Entwicklungspolitik bleibt wichtig und bietet öffentliche Finanzierungsmöglichkeiten sowie Instrumente zur Bewältigung lokaler und globaler Herausforderungen. Gleichzeitig steht sie unter strukturellem Druck und ist Gegenstand von Reformdebatten. item.content:encoded:
Inter- and Transnational Cooperation

发布源: German Development Institute --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-26

Global policies for sustainable futures depend on cross-border cooperation to address risks like poverty, inequality, conflicts, public health, and climate change. This requires both intergovernmental collaboration, through platforms like the UN and G20, and transnational engagement involving non-governmental actors, such as civil society, the private sector, and research communities. Recent geopolitical shifts and conflicts have strengthened the collective identity of Global South alliances, like the G77 and BRICS, while Western alliances face reinvigoration, often viewing these shifts as systemic rivalry.

Our department analyses diverse forms of cooperation, including North-South, South-South, and triangular partnerships, with a focus on the political economy of cooperation structures and development policy. We examine evolving concepts like “Global South” and explore innovative cooperation examples, such as inter-urban collaboration in Arctic regions. Development policy remains vital, providing public financing and tools to address local and global challenges, yet it faces structural pressure and debates over reform. Future research will focus on how geopolitical and geo-economic dynamics shape global de global development agendas and cooperation structures for sustainable futures.

Our Postgraduate Programme for Sustainability Cooperation (PGP) enhances the competence of master’s graduates aspiring to a career in international cooperation for development and sustainability. The Postgraduate Programme offers a comprehensive 360-degree perspective on global cooperation, and participants learn competences for partnership-based cooperation. Participants gain a foundation for reflective and dedicated professional action and are part of our valuable network. Thus, the Programme is more than just a gateway into a career.

Each year, we select 18 people for our 9-month programme.

How does cooperation in partnership work?

In the Programme, you will strengthen your cooperation skills through intensive teamwork and collaboration with our international partners. The Programme continuously fosters opportunities for meaningful encounters and exchange. We not only teach cooperation, we live it.

How do research findings influence policy-making?

At IDOS, we work empirically at the interface between science, policy and development practice. Our participants gain experience in theory-led and empirically based policy advice as a basis for political decision-making. This proximity to political decision-making processes makes the Postgraduate Programme at IDOS unique.

Part of our research in the period 2024 to 2026 will be organised in four working groups. They focus on transversal topics, allowing us to draw together diverse expertise and perspectives from across SWP’s research divisions. These topics embrace fundamental questions of great complexity and political urgency. Our research will explore interconnections, impacts, conflicts of goals and options for action. The transversal topics form part of SWP’s currentframework for research(in German only). In this document SWP outlines issues and challenges facing German foreign and security policy and why and how to address them.

item.content:encoded:
Militarisation and Arms Control

发布源: Bonn International Center for Conversion (BICC) --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-26

bicc projects in this topic focus on the effects of militarisation and weapons proliferation. bicc’s work aims to reduce their negative impact by strengthening arms control measures at various levels of society.

The accessibility and quality of weaponry significantly impact the motivations and prospects for engaging in acts of violence. They affect the probability of engaging in violent conflict and influence the actions of state and non-state entities involved. bicc researches the diverse consequences of armament, militarisation and weapons control at various levels to reduce their potentially detrimental impact on societies.

First, we map the global dynamics of militarisation as reflected in government defence spending, armed forces personnel and heavy weapons systems. In doing so, we advance knowledge of the so-called security–development nexus by researching how militarisation affects development.

Second, we are curious about the local consequences of militarisation and international arms and technology transfers, with a special focus on developing countries and regions of conflict.

We are particularly interested in the effects of arms transfers on regional conflicts and human rights, as well as changes in military-government and military–society ties.

item.content:encoded:
Building Peace and Social Cohesion

发布源: Bonn International Center for Conversion (BICC) --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-26

This topic brings together bicc’s research on the potentials for peace within societies. Projects within this topic aim to understand actor experiences and perceptions to identify common or competing visions of peace and social cohesion.

In various regions across the globe, societies are characterised by numerous sources of conflict that arise from interconnected political, religious, ethnic and economic factors.

The research conducted at bicc seeks to understand how social cohesion can be enhanced and contribute to peace in different contexts such as states, societies and local communities. Our research is grounded in the empirical data derived from the experiences and subjective perceptions of individuals actively involved in these conflicts. Additionally, our research acknowledges the existence of contrasting perspectives on social cohesion while seeking to identify areas where consensus can be reached through negotiation, with the ultimate goal of fortifying peace.

Occasionally, a critical analysis of prevailing normative assumptions on the efficacy of peacebuilding institutions and practices, such as the role of the state, becomes necessary. The primary focus of our research is to examine the various tensions within societies and to explore the prospects for achieving peace within these settings. item.content:encoded:
Agents and Patterns of Security and War

发布源: Bonn International Center for Conversion (BICC) --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-26

bicc’s research on agents and patterns of security and war looks into the mechanisms of organised violence. Projects contributing to this topic explore how individuals and groups secure themselves, how violence is used at different levels of social organisation and the possible implications of transforming the conduct of war.

The analysis of organised violence's practices and structures is a critical component in understanding violent conflicts. The topic at hand pertains to the means by which individuals safeguard themselves against acts of violence and the mechanisms through which they engage in collective acts of violence against others.

bicc investigates practices of security-making and war-making at various levels of social organisation. We examine the various strategies vulnerable groups employ to protect themselves from external threats in their daily routines. Likewise, we critically reflect on the—often violent—practices of securitisation, which may secure some individuals but make others less secure.

Additionally, we also examine the ongoing changes in the conduct of combat to gain an understanding of their broader social, political and ethical ramifications.

The availability of novel technologies, as well as their application to warfare and mobility control, is reshaping military theory and practice across the world, not only in Western countries. Banz Monastery, with its 900 years of history, is located in the valley of the River Main in Upper Franconia. In about 1069 or 1071, Countess Alberada and her husband, Margrave Hermann of Vohburg, donated their castle on Mount Banz to the Benedictines as a monastery.In the Thirty Year War, the abbey was destroyed; between 1698 and 1780, it was rebuilt and extended first by Leonhard Dientzenhofer, and then, after his death, by Johann Dientzenhofer and Balthasar Neumann, to become one of the biggest monasteries in Bavaria. When the abbey closed as a result of secularisation, the monastery’s last glorious era came to an end. In 1814, Duke Wilhelm of Bavaria acquired Banz as his summer residence. Before being taken over by the Hanns Seidel Foundation as a meeting and education center in 1978, the monastery was in the possession of the missionary order of the „Society of the Holy Angels“. After extensive renovation and restoration work, the completion of Banz Monastery was celebrated in 1990.There are now 180 beds available for participants attending events; for conference work, there are twelve seminar rooms for groups of 15 to 300 persons. 发布源: Institute for Advanced Sustainability Studies --Germany | 抓取时间: 2026-11-26

A statement by researchers

The last draft of the cover decision presented by the COP31 Presidency was sharply criticized and rejected by several countries, including the EU member states.

The failure to reach a final declaration that combined consensus with ambition is a serious setback for multilateralism and climate action. With populist and nationalist forces on the rise, cooperation between states will remain indispensable. Nevertheless, we consider the rejection of the text by the EU, the Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and other countries to be a logical reaction.

The final draft of the cover decision contained no concrete language on fossil fuels, apart from a weak, indirect reference to the outcome of COP28 in Dubai, which called for a 'transition away from fossil fuels'.

The draft also placed unrealistic expectations on technologies such as carbon capture and storage (CCS) and carbon capture and utilization (CCU), without adequately accounting for their limits and risks. One example is enhanced oil recovery (EOR), in which captured CO₂ is injected into mature oil fields to extract additional oil. The text would thus have provided a pretext for using fossil fuels for longer than is compatible with climate targets.

Nor did the draft contain the binding commitments on clean power generation needed to make the COP's central goal – raising the share of electricity in global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 – effective for climate protection.

This blog was jointly developed byThomas Bruhn(RIFS),Thomas Kühn(International Psychoanalytic University Berlin), andJeremy Dommnich(The Hague University of Applied Sciences). It is written from Thomas Bruhn’s personal perspective, while drawing on shared research, conversations, and reflections among the three authors.

This question has – once again – been on my mind during the past days at COP. After more than three decades of international climate negotiations, with global emissions still far from the trajectories needed to avoid dangerous climate change, it seems legitimate to ask: Why do we keep organizing these enormous gatherings? What is their actual contribution to addressing the climate crisis? And what happens here that could not happen elsewhere?

Yesterday, in a conversation with two colleagues, we found ourselves approaching these questions from an unexpected angle. Over the past years, we have interviewed numerous people involved in the international climate negotiations, exploring their experiences of leadership, responsibility, and agency. What emerges is a deeply paradoxical picture. Many negotiators understand themselves as exercising leadership, yet struggle to identify where they can actually make a difference. They carry significant responsibilities while operating within highly structured processes that leave remarkably little room for individual agency.

Our scientists are driven to find answers to the big questions of our times. In tackling their field in scientific frontier research they need courage, talent, persistence - and your unique support!

Excellent frontier research is a high risk mission, requiring high trust, too. The results are at times not predictable, nonetheless this search is what drives us to push forward and exceed boundaries of knowledge. And knowledge is essential for progress: technologies and medical care improve our lives and ensure economic prosperity. Therefore, research in Germany is largely state-funded, because knowledge is a publicly invaluable good.

Nevertheless, public funding alone at times does not suffice, as our scientists find themselves in a tough international competition. Max Planck Society can only stand up to and succeed when donors support our research, too.

Here, our Major Donors, ourSupporting Membersand ourBoards of Trusteesset benchmarks. And because our world class scientists need that extra head room (especially when public funding ist not available), we are generously supported by theMax Planck Foundation.

Excellent frontier research also requires outstanding support. Succeeding as a visionary is part of your set of beliefs.

Join us on this frontier journey - you are in best company.
